title: Introduction to Abstract Data Types (ADT)
overview: An abstract data type (ADT) packages some data together with the operations allowed on it. At AS level the three ADTs are the stack (last in, first out), the queue (first in, first out) and the linked list (items kept in order by pointers rather than by position). You are not asked to write pseudocode for them. Instead Paper 1 questions give you a diagram or a pair of arrays and ask you to add, edit or delete items, fill in the new contents and pointer values, describe how an array implements the structure, or justify which structure suits a situation. Marks depend on updating every pointer correctly at every step: the top-of-stack pointer, the front and end pointers of a queue (including wrap-around in a circular queue), and the start pointer, free-list pointer and node pointers of a linked list.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding that an ADT is a collection of data and a set of operations on those data.
Show understanding that a stack, queue and linked list are examples of ADTs, and describe the key features of a stack, queue and linked list and justify their use for a given situation.
Use a stack, queue and linked list to store data, including adding, editing and deleting data (candidates will not be required to write pseudocode for these structures).
Describe how a queue, stack and linked list can be implemented using arrays.

definitions.definition: A collection of data together with the set of operations that can be carried out on that data, such as create, add, find, delete and traverse, described without depending on how it is stored.
A last-in, first-out (LIFO) ADT: items are added (pushed) and removed (popped) only at one end, the top.
A first-in, first-out (FIFO) ADT: items join at the end (rear) and leave from the front, so they are removed in the order they arrived.
A queue held in a fixed-size array whose front and end pointers go back to the first element after passing the last one, so slots freed by removals are reused without moving any data.
An ADT made of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node, so the logical order is set by the pointers rather than by where the nodes are stored.
One element of a linked list: its data (often a key field plus other fields) and its pointer field.
A variable or field that holds the address (in an array implementation, the index) of the node it refers to.
A pointer value that refers to no node, marking the end of a list or an empty list; in an array implementation it is often shown as -1.
A variable that holds the address of the first node of a linked list; it is null when the list is empty.
A second linked list that chains together all unused nodes in the array, with its own free-list pointer, so a spare node can be found at once when data is added.
Overflow is trying to add to a structure that is already full; underflow is trying to remove from one that is empty.

sections.title: What an abstract data type is
content: An abstract data type (ADT) is a collection of data plus the operations you are allowed to perform on it. The typical operations are: create a new, empty instance; add (insert) an item; find an item; delete an item; and go through all items in an organised way. The word abstract means the ADT is described by what it does, not by how the data is laid out in memory. The same stack could be built from an array or from a linked list, and a program using it would not notice the difference.

The three ADTs in this topic differ mainly in where items may be added and removed. A stack only allows access at one end. A queue adds at one end and removes at the other. A linked list keeps items in a chosen order and allows adding and removing anywhere. In the examples below each item is a single letter, but in real use each item would usually be a record with many fields.
bullets: ADT = data + the set of operations on that data.
Common operations: create, add, find, delete, access every item in turn.
The stack, queue and linked list are all ADTs; each can be implemented with arrays.

sections.title: The stack and its array implementation
content: A stack is like a pile of trays: a new tray goes on the top, and the only tray you can take is the one on top. The item added most recently is the first to be removed, which is called last in, first out (LIFO). Adding an item is called a push and removing one is called a pop.

A stack is implemented with a 1D array and two pointers. BaseOfStackPointer always holds the index of the first slot (0 below). TopOfStackPointer holds the index of the item most recently pushed, and is -1 when the stack is empty. To push, check that the stack is not full, add 1 to the top pointer, then store the item there. To pop, check that the stack is not empty, take the item at the top pointer, then subtract 1. A popped value is often left in the array, but it is no longer part of the stack and will be overwritten by the next push. Only the top item can be edited, by overwriting the element at TopOfStackPointer; anything lower down is reached only by popping the items above it.
bullets: LIFO: push and pop happen only at the top.
Array implementation: DECLARE Stack : ARRAY[0:4] OF CHAR with BaseOfStackPointer = 0 and TopOfStackPointer = -1 when empty.
Push: if not full, TopOfStackPointer + 1, then store. Pop: if not empty, read, then TopOfStackPointer - 1.
Pushing onto a full stack is overflow; popping an empty stack is underflow.

examples.label: Worked example: stack states in ARRAY[0:4] (- = unused slot, (x) = old value no longer in the stack)
examples.content:
Operation | [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] | Top | Notes
start     |  -   -   -   -   -  | -1  | empty
Push A    |  A   -   -   -   -  |  0  |
Push B    |  A   B   -   -   -  |  1  |
Push C    |  A   B   C   -   -  |  2  |
Pop       |  A   B  (C)  -   -  |  1  | returns C
Push D    |  A   B   D   -   -  |  2  | D overwrites old C
Push E    |  A   B   D   E   -  |  3  |
Push F    |  A   B   D   E   F  |  4  | Top = upper bound: full
Push G    |  A   B   D   E   F  |  4  | overflow - G rejected
Pop       |  A   B   D   E  (F) |  3  | returns F

BaseOfStackPointer stays 0 throughout. Items leave in the reverse of arrival order: C was the last in before the first pop, F the last in before the second.

examples.label: Illustration only (not required at AS): the push steps
examples.content:
IF TopOfStackPointer = 4 THEN
   OUTPUT "Stack full"
ELSE
   TopOfStackPointer ← TopOfStackPointer + 1
   Stack[TopOfStackPointer] ← NewItem
ENDIF

sections.title: Where a stack is the right choice
content: Choose a stack whenever the most recent item must be dealt with first, or when an order needs reversing. An undo feature pushes each action as the user makes it; pressing undo pops the latest action and reverses it, so actions are undone newest first. A web browser's back button works the same way with the pages visited.

When a program calls a procedure or function, the return address and local values are pushed onto a call stack, and popped when the subroutine finishes. This is how nested and recursive calls return in the correct order. Stacks are also used to reverse a sequence (push every item, then pop them all) and to evaluate expressions. A stack would be a poor choice for anything that must be served in order of arrival, such as print jobs, because the earliest item would wait longest.
bullets: Undo and back-button history: the newest action or page comes back first.
Subroutine calls and recursion: return addresses are pushed on call and popped on return.
Reversing data: push items in order, pop them in reverse order.
Justify a stack by pointing to the need for last-in, first-out access.

sections.title: The queue and a simple (linear) array implementation
content: A queue behaves like people waiting at a ticket desk: newcomers join at the end and people are served from the front, and nobody pushes in or leaves from the middle. The first item in is the first out (FIFO). Adding is often called enqueue and removing is called dequeue.

The simplest array version keeps the front of the queue fixed at index 0. EndOfQueuePointer holds the index of the last item and is -1 when the queue is empty. To add, check the queue is not full, add 1 to EndOfQueuePointer and store the item there. To remove, take the item at index 0, then move every remaining item one place towards the front and subtract 1 from EndOfQueuePointer. It works, but shifting every item on each removal is slow for a long queue, which is why the circular queue is normally used.
bullets: FIFO: add at the end, remove from the front.
Linear version: front fixed at index 0, EndOfQueuePointer = -1 when empty.
Every removal shifts all other items forward one place, which wastes time.
Adding to a full queue is overflow; removing from an empty queue is underflow.

examples.label: Worked example: linear queue in ARRAY[0:4] with the front fixed at 0
examples.content:
Operation | [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] | EndOfQueuePointer
start     |  -   -   -   -   -  | -1
Join A    |  A   -   -   -   -  |  0
Join B    |  A   B   -   -   -  |  1
Join C    |  A   B   C   -   -  |  2
Leave     |  B   C   -   -   -  |  1   (A removed; B and C each moved up one slot)
Join D    |  B   C   D   -   -  |  2

The single removal needed two data moves; with 1000 items waiting it would need 999.

sections.title: The circular queue
content: A circular queue avoids moving data. Both ends move instead: FrontOfQueuePointer holds the index of the item that will leave next, and EndOfQueuePointer holds the index of the item that joined last. When either pointer is at the last index of the array and must advance, it goes back to index 0, so the array behaves as if its two ends were joined into a ring. A counter, NumberInQueue, makes full and empty easy to detect: the queue is full when it equals the array size and empty when it is 0.

To add: if NumberInQueue equals the size, report overflow; otherwise move EndOfQueuePointer on one place (wrapping from the last index to 0), store the item and add 1 to the counter. To remove: if the counter is 0, report underflow; otherwise take the item at FrontOfQueuePointer, move that pointer on one place (again wrapping) and subtract 1 from the counter. Slots emptied at the front are reused by later additions without any shifting. At the start FrontOfQueuePointer = 0, EndOfQueuePointer = -1 and NumberInQueue = 0. In a queue, only an item's data can be edited in place; items are never added or removed anywhere except at the two ends.
bullets: Front and end pointers both advance; after the last index they wrap to 0 (e.g. Pointer ← (Pointer + 1) MOD Size).
A count of items tells full (count = size) from empty (count = 0).
No data is shifted, so removal takes the same time however long the queue is.
Justify a queue whenever items must be handled in order of arrival: print jobs, keyboard buffers, customer requests, processes waiting for the CPU.

examples.label: Worked example: circular queue in ARRAY[0:5] (6 slots). (x) = old value no longer in the queue
examples.content:
Operation | [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] | Front | End | Count | Notes
start     |  -   -   -   -   -   -  |  0    | -1  |  0    | empty
Join A    |  A   -   -   -   -   -  |  0    |  0  |  1    |
Join B    |  A   B   -   -   -   -  |  0    |  1  |  2    |
Join C    |  A   B   C   -   -   -  |  0    |  2  |  3    |
Join D    |  A   B   C   D   -   -  |  0    |  3  |  4    |
Join E    |  A   B   C   D   E   -  |  0    |  4  |  5    |
Leave     | (A)  B   C   D   E   -  |  1    |  4  |  4    | returns A
Leave     | (A) (B)  C   D   E   -  |  2    |  4  |  3    | returns B
Join F    | (A) (B)  C   D   E   F  |  2    |  5  |  4    | End reaches last index
Join G    |  G  (B)  C   D   E   F  |  2    |  0  |  5    | End wraps 5 -> 0
Join H    |  G   H   C   D   E   F  |  2    |  1  |  6    | Count = 6: full
Join I    |  G   H   C   D   E   F  |  2    |  1  |  6    | overflow - I rejected
Leave     |  G   H  (C)  D   E   F  |  3    |  1  |  5    | returns C

Queue from front to end now: D, E, F, G, H (indexes 3, 4, 5, 0, 1). The next Join would go into index 2, reusing C's old slot.

sections.title: Linked lists: nodes, pointers and the start pointer
content: In an ordinary array used as a list (a linear list), items sit in consecutive locations, so keeping them in order means moving data around. A linked list lets each item be stored in any free location and joins the items into the required order with pointers. Each item is a node made of a data part and a pointer to the next node. A start pointer holds the address of the first node, and the last node's pointer is the null pointer, meaning there is no next node. An empty list has a null start pointer.

To traverse the list, begin at the node the start pointer refers to, process its data, follow its pointer to the next node, and carry on until the null pointer is reached. There is no direct jump to, say, the fourth item: it can only be reached by following the chain. This makes searching slower than in an array, and each node needs extra space for its pointer, but it makes insertion and deletion much cheaper.
bullets: Node = data + pointer to the next node; order is decided by the pointers, not the storage position.
Start pointer gives the first node; the null pointer marks the end.
Traversal follows the pointers from the start pointer until null.
Costs: extra memory for pointers and sequential-only access.

sections.title: Adding and deleting nodes by changing pointers
content: Because order comes from pointers, adding or removing a node only changes one or two pointers; no other data moves. Four cases are worth learning. Add at the start: copy the start pointer into the new node's pointer, then point the start pointer at the new node. Add at the end: set the old last node's pointer to the new node and give the new node the null pointer. Insert between two nodes: copy the earlier node's pointer into the new node, then point the earlier node at the new node. The order of these two steps matters; doing them the other way round loses the rest of the list.

Delete the first node: copy its pointer into the start pointer. Delete the last node: set the previous node's pointer to null. Delete a node in the middle: copy the deleted node's pointer into the previous node's pointer, so the chain skips it. The data of a deleted node may still be in memory, but nothing points to it, so it is no longer in the list. Editing a node means finding it by traversal and overwriting its data; if the list is kept in order and the new value would belong somewhere else, delete the node and insert the new value instead.
bullets: Insert between P and Q: New.pointer ← P.pointer, then P.pointer ← New.
Delete X after P: P.pointer ← X.pointer (for the first node: StartPointer ← X.pointer).
No data values move, which saves time when records are large.
Edit: traverse to the node and overwrite its data, re-inserting if the sort order would change.

examples.label: Worked example (conceptual): an alphabetical list D -> M -> T
examples.content:
Start -> D -> M -> T -> null

Insert G between D and M:
  1. G.pointer ← D.pointer   (G now points to M)
  2. D.pointer ← G           (D now points to G)
  Start -> D -> G -> M -> T -> null

Delete M (between G and T):
  G.pointer ← M.pointer      (G now points to T)
  Start -> D -> G -> T -> null

Delete D (the first node):
  Start ← D.pointer          (Start now points to G)
  Start -> G -> T -> null

sections.title: Implementing a linked list with arrays
content: A linked list can be built from two 1D arrays of the same size: a Data array and a Pointer array. Reading across one index gives one node: Data[i] is the node's data and Pointer[i] is the index of the next node. StartPointer is an integer variable holding the index of the first node, and -1 is used as the null pointer. Instead of two arrays, one array of records, each with a data field and a pointer field, does the same job.

Adding a value puts it into any unused element of the Data array, then adjusts pointers so the node appears at the correct place in the chain. Deleting a value only changes pointers; the old data can stay in the array because no pointer reaches it. This keeps the list in order without ever moving the stored data. Unlike a dynamic linked list, an array-based one has a fixed maximum size set by the array bounds.
bullets: Two parallel arrays (Data and Pointer) or one array of records; each index is one node.
StartPointer holds the index of the first node; -1 is the null pointer.
Traverse: Current ← StartPointer, then repeatedly use Data[Current] and Current ← Pointer[Current] until Current = -1.
The array bounds fix the maximum number of nodes.

examples.label: Worked example: reading an array-based list
examples.content:
StartPointer = 1

Index | Data | Pointer
[0]   |  M   |   2
[1]   |  D   |   3
[2]   |  T   |  -1
[3]   |  G   |   0

Traversal: Start 1 -> Data[1] = D, Pointer 3 -> Data[3] = G, Pointer 0 -> Data[0] = M, Pointer 2 -> Data[2] = T, Pointer -1 -> stop
Output order: D, G, M, T (alphabetical), although the data is stored as M, D, T, G.

sections.title: The free list: tracking unused nodes
content: To add a node quickly, the program needs to know which array elements are unused. The answer is to link all the spare elements into a second linked list, the free list, with its own FreeListPointer. When the arrays are first set up, the linked list is empty (StartPointer = -1) and every element is on the free list: FreeListPointer = 0, each Pointer[i] = i + 1, and the last element's pointer is -1.

To add a value: check FreeListPointer is not -1 (otherwise the list is full); take the node it points to; move FreeListPointer on to that node's old pointer; store the data; then link the node into the main list at the correct place. To delete a value: unlink the node from the main list as usual, then return it to the front of the free list by setting its pointer to the current FreeListPointer and making FreeListPointer point to it. Nodes that are freed are the first to be reused.
bullets: Initial state: StartPointer = -1, FreeListPointer = 0, Pointer[i] = i + 1, last pointer = -1.
Add: take the first free node, advance FreeListPointer, store data, link into the list.
Delete: unlink from the list, then push the node onto the front of the free list.
FreeListPointer = -1 means no space is left.

examples.label: Worked example: alphabetical linked list in Data[0:6] / Pointer[0:6] with a free list
examples.content:
Pointer array shown as [0..6]; S = StartPointer, F = FreeListPointer, null = -1

Step       | Data [0..6]           | Pointer [0..6]            | S  | F  | List
start      | - - - - - - -         | 1  2  3  4  5  6 -1       | -1 | 0  | (empty)
add M      | M - - - - - -         | -1 2  3  4  5  6 -1       | 0  | 1  | M
add D      | M D - - - - -         | -1 0  3  4  5  6 -1       | 1  | 2  | D M
add T      | M D T - - - -         | 2  0 -1  4  5  6 -1       | 1  | 3  | D M T
add G      | M D T G - - -         | 2  3 -1  0  5  6 -1       | 1  | 4  | D G M T
delete M   | M D T G - - -         | 4  3 -1  2  5  6 -1       | 1  | 0  | D G T
delete D   | M D T G - - -         | 4  0 -1  2  5  6 -1       | 3  | 1  | G T
edit T->P  | M D P G - - -         | 4  0 -1  2  5  6 -1       | 3  | 1  | G P
add K      | M K P G - - -         | 4  2 -1  1  5  6 -1       | 3  | 0  | G K P

Checks:
- add G: G goes in free node 3 (F moves to Pointer[3] = 4); G.pointer ← D.pointer = 0; D.pointer (Pointer[1]) ← 3.
- delete M (index 0, after G): Pointer[3] ← Pointer[0] = 2; then M's node joins the free list: Pointer[0] ← F = 4, F ← 0.
- delete D (first node, index 1): S ← Pointer[1] = 3; Pointer[1] ← F = 0, F ← 1.
- edit T->P keeps alphabetical order (G < P), so only Data[2] changes.
- add K reuses node 1: F ← Pointer[1] = 0; K goes between G and P: Pointer[1] ← Pointer[3] = 2, Pointer[3] ← 1.
Final free list: 0 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> null. Old values M (index 0) remain in Data but are not reachable from S.

sections.title: Stacks and queues built on linked lists, and choosing a structure
content: A linked list can itself be used to implement the other two ADTs. For a stack, treat the start pointer as the top: always add a new node at the start and always remove the node at the start. For a queue, treat the start pointer as the front: add new nodes at the end of the list and remove nodes from the start. In both cases only the permitted operations are used, so the list behaves exactly like a stack or a queue.

When justifying a structure, link a feature of the ADT to a need in the scenario. Use a stack when the last item stored must be the first retrieved (undo, back button, subroutine returns, reversing). Use a queue when items must be processed in the order they arrived and nobody may jump ahead (print spooling, buffers, job scheduling), and a circular queue when this must be done in a fixed amount of memory without moving data. Use a linked list when items must be kept in a sorted order while being frequently added or removed anywhere, because only pointers change; accept that it needs extra space for pointers and must be searched from the start.
bullets: Stack from a linked list: add and remove only at the start node (start pointer = top).
Queue from a linked list: add at the end, remove from the start (start pointer = front).
Justify with the access rule the task needs: newest first (stack), oldest first (queue), ordered with frequent insert and delete anywhere (linked list).

comparisonTable.title: Stack, queue and linked list compared
rows: LIFO: add and remove at the top only
1D array + BaseOfStackPointer and TopOfStackPointer (-1 when empty)
Push: check not full, top + 1, store
Pop: check not empty, read, top - 1
Undo, back button, subroutine calls, reversing
FIFO: add at the end, remove from the front
1D array + FrontOfQueuePointer, EndOfQueuePointer and a count; pointers wrap to 0
Check not full, end moves on one (wrapping), store
Check not empty, read at front, front moves on one (wrapping)
Print queue, keyboard buffer, job scheduling
Any position; order set by pointers
Data array + Pointer array (or array of records), StartPointer, FreeListPointer, -1 as null
Take a free node, store data, update two pointers
Redirect one pointer, return node to the free list
Sorted lists with frequent insertion and deletion

diagram.title: Stack states in ARRAY[0:4] (TopOfStackPointer shown)
nodes: Push A, B, C: [A, B, C], Top = 2
Push D, E, F: [A, B, D, E, F], Top = 4 (full)
Pop returns F: [A, B, D, E], Top = 3

analysisChains.title: Why a simple queue reports full when it is not
steps: A queue in ARRAY[0:5] never moves its data and never wraps its pointers
Six items join, so the end pointer reaches index 5; then four items leave, so the front pointer is at index 4
Only two items are in the queue, yet a new item cannot be added because the end pointer is already at the last index
Indexes 0 to 3 are empty but unreachable
analysisChains.evaluation: Making the queue circular fixes this: the end pointer wraps from 5 to 0, so the next item goes into index 0. Using a count of items rather than pointer positions to test for full means the queue is only full when all six slots hold waiting items.

analysisChains.title: Choosing a structure for a printer shared by a class
steps: Twenty students send documents to one printer at different times
Fairness requires the earliest document to be printed first
A stack would print the most recent document first, so early jobs could wait indefinitely
A queue removes items in the order they were added
analysisChains.evaluation: A queue (FIFO) is justified because print jobs must be handled in order of arrival; a circular queue in a fixed array lets the spooler reuse slots as jobs finish without moving the waiting jobs.

analysisChains.title: Why a sorted list of large records suits a linked list
steps: A library keeps 5000 book records in title order and adds or withdraws books every day
In a sorted array, inserting a title near the start means moving thousands of whole records along one place
In a linked list, the new record goes into any free node and only two pointers change; a deletion changes one pointer
The cost is one extra pointer per node and searching by following pointers from the start
analysisChains.evaluation: Because insertions and deletions are frequent and the records are large, a linked list is justified: it keeps title order without moving data. An array would be better only if records were rarely changed and fast direct access by position was the main need.

examTips: When asked to show a structure after an operation, write out the whole array and every pointer value, not just the item that changed.
Take pointer conventions from the question (e.g. whether the top pointer shows the last item or the next free slot, and whether null is -1 or 0) and use them consistently.
For a circular queue, show the end or front pointer wrapping to 0 explicitly and check for full before every addition.
For linked-list insertion, state the two pointer changes in the correct order: new node's pointer first, then the previous node's pointer.
When justifying a structure, name the feature (LIFO, FIFO, pointer-based ordering) and link it to a specific need in the scenario.
commonMistakes: Mixing up LIFO and FIFO, e.g. removing the oldest item from a stack.
Forgetting to change the pointer (top, front or end) after adding or removing an item.
Not wrapping a circular queue's pointer back to 0, or treating a wrapped queue as full when slots are free.
In a linked-list insertion, changing the previous node's pointer first and losing the link to the rest of the list.
Forgetting to return a deleted node to the free list, or to advance FreeListPointer when a node is used.
Thinking deleted data must be erased from the array: only the pointers need to change.

quickRecall.question: What is an ADT?
quickRecall.answer: A collection of data together with a set of operations on that data (e.g. create, add, find, delete, traverse).

quickRecall.question: Stack ARRAY[0:4] holds A, B, D, E with TopOfStackPointer = 3. What changes after a pop?
quickRecall.answer: E is returned and TopOfStackPointer becomes 2; the stack is A, B, D (E may remain in the array but is no longer in the stack).

quickRecall.question: What values does an empty stack's top pointer and an empty circular queue's pointers take in this note's convention?
Why is a circular queue better than a linear queue with the front fixed at index 0?
quickRecall.answer: No data has to be moved when an item leaves; the pointers move and wrap round, so freed slots at the start are reused.

quickRecall.question: In ARRAY[0:5], EndOfQueuePointer = 5 and the queue is not full. Where does the next item go?
quickRecall.answer: Index 0: the end pointer wraps from the last index back to the first.

quickRecall.question: How is node N inserted after node P in a linked list?
quickRecall.answer: Copy P's pointer into N's pointer, then set P's pointer to N.

quickRecall.question: What is the free list and what are its initial pointer values in Pointer[0:6]?
quickRecall.answer: A linked list of unused nodes; FreeListPointer = 0 and Pointer = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, -1, with StartPointer = -1.

quickRecall.question: Give a situation for each of stack, queue and linked list.
quickRecall.answer: Stack: undo feature (newest first). Queue: print jobs (oldest first). Linked list: a sorted list that changes often (only pointers change).
